_readme: This is the whole dictionary. Add a word by adding an object to "terms" and running: python3 build.py. Fields: term (required), aka, definition (string or list of paragraphs), plainly, tags, seeAlso, emoji, post (the URL of the LinkedIn post that introduced this term, shown as a link on its term page). Each letter's page automatically lists every distinct post its terms cite, in the order those terms first appear — no separate list to maintain.

site.title: A–Z Competition Law Dictionary
site.tagline: Australian competition law, one friendly word at a time.
site.description: A cheerful, plain-English dictionary of Australian competition law terms, published one letter at a time from A to Z.

definition: A legal framework within competition law that allows third-party businesses to use essential infrastructure owned by a competitor on reasonable terms and conditions.
Examples found in rail, wheat export and telecommunications networks.
Otherwise known as the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.
Federal regulator of competition and consumer law in Australia.
Otherwise known as the Australian Consumer Law.
Federal legislation for consumer law regulation in Australia - found in Schedule 2 of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth).
All the communications that businesses (and sometimes influencers) use to attract attention to their products and services, with the goal of maximising customer conversion and revenue.
Key focus area for many misleading or deceptive conduct claims.
Often used in overseas jurisdictions including the United States to refer to the practice of competition law.
Refers to rules and laws that promote fair competition between businesses.
A public pathway involving an ACCC application to protect conduct you are about to engage in that may otherwise contravene competition laws.
Depending on the conduct, you need to prove either: 1. the conduct is not likely to substantially lessen competition; or 2. the conduct is likely to result in a net public benefit.
One of many examples of misleading advertising practices.
Products or services are advertised at a very cheap price to attract your interest as a consumer.
BUT when you go to buy, the products are 'out of stock' (meaning the business may never have stocked a reasonable quantity to be able to sell for a reasonable time to begin with).
A remedy that can resolve competition concerns in a merger or acquisition.
Court enforceable and rarely accepted by the regulator.

Involves a commitment to do or refrain from doing certain actions. For example, anti-discrimination obligations, or limits on the ability of the merged entity to increase price / decrease quality for a period of time.
A form of cartel conduct, also known as collusive tendering.
Competitors agreeing what bids to submit to determine the winner in advance.
Examples: not bidding at all, taking turns at winning bids, or bidding above a minimum 'floor'.
When parties agree or act together to refuse to supply or acquire goods or services, or prevent a third party from doing so.
High risk conduct. May amount to cartel conduct or some other contravention of competition law.
Very rarely authorised by the ACCC.
